## Warm-up retrieval

::: {.mcq data-correct="c"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q1. What does it mean to construct a 95% confidence interval?</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>There is a 95% probability that the population parameter lies in the interval</li>
  <li>95% of the data values fall in the interval</li>
  <li>If we repeated the procedure many times, about 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the true parameter</li>
  <li>The sample mean has a 95% chance of being correct</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(c)</strong> The 95% refers to the long-run reliability of the *procedure*, not the probability for any single computed interval. The parameter is fixed; the interval is random.</div>
:::

## Check-in: Tying confidence intervals to hypothesis testing

::: {.predict}
Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.
:::

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q1. A small *p*-value (e.g., $p = 0.001$) means:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>The null hypothesis is true with probability 0.001</li>
  <li>The data would be unusual if the null hypothesis were true</li>
  <li>The alternative hypothesis is proven</li>
  <li>The chance the next study will replicate this result is high</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> $p$-values measure how surprising the data is *under* $H_0$, not the probability that $H_0$ is true. A small $p$-value is evidence against $H_0$, but it doesn't *prove* $H_a$ and doesn't tell you anything about the magnitude of the effect.</div>
:::

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q2. A *Type I error* occurs when:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>You correctly reject the null hypothesis</li>
  <li>You reject a true null hypothesis (a &quot;false positive&quot;)</li>
  <li>You fail to reject a false null hypothesis</li>
  <li>You measure something incorrectly</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> Type I = rejecting $H_0$ when it's actually true. Probability is the significance level $\alpha$ (commonly 0.05). Type II = failing to reject $H_0$ when it's actually false.</div>
:::

## Check-in: Understanding hypothesis tests

::: {.predict}
Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.
:::

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q3. A permutation test computes the $p$-value as &quot;share of *null* statistics at least as extreme as the observed one.&quot; For a **two-sided** alternative $H_A: \mu \neq \mu_0$, &quot;as extreme as&quot; means:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>Greater than the observed value only</li>
  <li>**At least as far from the null center as the observed value, in *either* direction** (so statistics that are unusually high *or* unusually low both count)</li>
  <li>Less than the observed value only</li>
  <li>Equal to the observed value exactly</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> A two-sided alternative cares about extremity in *both* tails — equally surprising whether the observed sample mean lands far above or far below $\mu_0$. The one-sided variants ($H_A: \mu > \mu_0$ or $H_A: \mu < \mu_0$) only count extremity in the *predicted* direction, so the resulting $p$-value is roughly half what you'd get from a two-sided test on the same data. The choice of one- vs two-sided must be made *before* looking at the data.</div>
:::

## Check-in: Conducting hypothesis tests

::: {.predict}
Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.
:::

::: {.mcq data-correct="a"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q4. A hypothesis test has $\alpha = 0.05$ and you obtain $p = 0.04$. The correct conclusion:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>**Reject $H_0$; the data are unusual under $H_0$**</li>
  <li>Accept $H_a$ (the alternative is proven)</li>
  <li>$H_0$ is false with 96% probability</li>
  <li>The result will replicate the same way in the next study</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(a)</strong> Be careful with wording. We *reject* $H_0$, not &quot;accept $H_a$&quot;. And $p = 0.04$ doesn't say anything about replicability or the magnitude of any difference — only about how surprising the data are if $H_0$ were exactly true.</div>
:::

## Check-in: Interpreting hypothesis tests

::: {.predict}
Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.
:::

::: {.mcq data-correct="c"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q5. Section 9.1 ties confidence intervals to hypothesis tests. A 95% CI for a parameter $\theta$ is $(2.1, 5.8)$. Which value of $\theta_0$ would the corresponding **two-sided** test fail to reject at $\alpha = 0.05$?</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>$\theta_0 = 0$</li>
  <li>$\theta_0 = 1$</li>
  <li>**$\theta_0 = 4$**</li>
  <li>$\theta_0 = 10$</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(c)</strong> The CI-test duality says: at level $\alpha$, a two-sided test rejects $H_0: \theta = \theta_0$ if and only if $\theta_0$ falls **outside** the corresponding $1 - \alpha$ CI. Since 4 lies *inside* the CI $(2.1, 5.8)$, the test fails to reject; the other three values lie outside and would be rejected. Useful shortcut: once you have a CI, you've effectively pre-computed the test for *every* candidate $\theta_0$ at once.</div>
:::

## Check-in: Case study: are action or romance movies rated higher?

::: {.predict}
Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.
:::

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q6. Increasing the **sample size** in a study primarily affects:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>The probability of Type I error</li>
  <li>**The probability of Type II error (lower with larger $n$)**</li>
  <li>The significance level $\alpha$</li>
  <li>Nothing</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> Larger $n$ → tighter sampling distribution → easier for the test to *detect* real differences from $H_0$ → lower Type II error rate (fewer &quot;fail to reject&quot; results when $H_0$ is actually false). Type I error is set by the chosen $\alpha$, not by $n$.</div>
:::

## Check-in: Summary and Final Remarks

::: {.predict}
Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.
:::

::: {.mcq data-correct="c"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q7. A research team reports a &quot;statistically significant&quot; result with $p = 0.03$ and $\alpha = 0.05$. Which of the following is the BEST interpretation of what the test has shown?</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>The truth is exactly $H_A$</li>
  <li>The probability the null is true is 0.03</li>
  <li>**The data are unlikely under $H_0$ — small enough to reject $H_0$ by the chapter's decision rule, but the test doesn't tell us *by how much* the truth differs from $H_0$**</li>
  <li>The null is definitively false</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(c)</strong> Hypothesis testing is *binary*: reject or fail to reject. A small $p$-value says the observed data would be rare if $H_0$ were exactly true, so by the decision rule we reject $H_0$. What the test *doesn't* tell you is how far off from $H_0$ the truth actually is — the gap could be tiny or large. (CIs from Chapter 8 are the tool for answering &quot;how much&quot;.)</div>
:::
